name: Butcher's broom (Ruscus aculeatus)
short: Case reports: diabetic ketoacidosis in a diabetic woman; chronic diarrhoea, colitis and 1 reversible kidney failure with a Ruscus combination product. 12-week trial (166 women): rated well tolerated.
text: In a 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 166 women with chronic venous insufficiency, an oral Ruscus extract was rated as well tolerated: of 48 adverse events across both groups, 22 occurred with Ruscus and one of these was considered related to the study medicine (rated unlikely). A case report describes a 39-year-old woman with diabetes who developed diabetic ketoacidosis, complicated by high potassium and severe acidosis, 5 days after starting butcher's broom for ankle swelling; the authors note that the plant contains substances with alpha-adrenergic stimulating properties. Case reports describe chronic diarrhoea, with weight loss, low potassium and, in one patient, reversible acute kidney failure, and lymphocytic colitis (in one patient, immune changes in the gut lining reappeared on rechallenge), in people taking a combination phlebotonic product used in France that contains Ruscus aculeatus with hesperidin methyl chalcone and ascorbic acid (named only by brand in the case abstracts); in the diarrhoea series, symptoms resolved whenever the product was stopped; the colitis abstract does not report the outcome after stopping, and the abstracts do not say which component was responsible. A 2025 review notes that much of the research on Ruscus is on such combination formulations, which makes it hard to attribute effects to Ruscus alone. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
